 Boulder, meet your first Sundance headliners
 Arts news: Natalie Portman, Stanley Tucci and Jesse Eisenberg head to Boulder. ... Another actor joins the bench. ... Opie Gone Bad reunites and more.
 By John Moore 
 Published November 18, 2026 7:05pm 
 + 
 Add Denver Gazette on Google
 Look who's coming to Sundance, from left: Jesse Eisenberg ('Now You See Me: Now You Don't), Natalie Portman ('Love and Darkness') and Stanley Tucci ('Submission). (Credits: midtcpress, Katalin Vermes/Lionsgate via AP, Great Point Media.) 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 It’s starting to look a lot like … not that . (Have you seen even a single flake of snow?)
 No, it’s starting to look a lot like … Sundance!
 Recommended Stories
 ▶

 We’re starting to learn which stars will be descending on Boulder for Colorado’s first Sundance Film Festival from Jan. 21-31. And the first three Colorado-bound bold-faced names we know are downright audacious -faced names: Natalie Portman, Stanley Tucci and Jesse Eisenberg.
 Portman will be here in partnership with Dior to present an inaugural award supporting the “creativity, boldness and vision” of women filmmakers. Tucci will emcee the nonprofit Sundance Institute’s annual fundraiser on Jan. 22 at the Limelight Hotel. At that party, Eisenberg will receive the festival’s annual Trailblazer Award.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Eisenberg wrote and directed “The Debut,” a musical comedy about community theater that stars Julianne Moore and was shown last month at the Denver Film Festival.
 The Miss Dior x Women at Sundance Institute Award, named after Catherine Dior (who inspired Christian Dior’s first fragrance), will recognize “a breakthrough cultural force whose bold vision is reshaping the filmmaking landscape.” It will go to “a talent on the rise who empowers women in film through disruptive storytelling and bold creative choices.”
 But we’re not telling you who it is because … we don’t know.
 Portman will present the award during the Women’s Celebration Brunch. We also don’t know when or where that will happen because … that has not been announced yet, either.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Just Natalie. Which is a pretty good start.
 “Supporting women storytellers is so important, not only because their voices deserve to be heard, but because they bring perspectives that enrich our understanding of the world,” Portman said in a statement. “When a belief in emotion, independence and conviction meets a commitment to authentic storytelling, we create more than opportunities for artists – we help ensure that women continue to shape culture through the stories they choose to tell.”
 What has been announced is the Women at Sundance Institute Miss Dior Momentum Fellowship, which will support six mid-career women artists working on their second or third independent feature films. The fellowship provides year-round creative and financial support through grants, mentorship, coaching, cohort gatherings and “a curated Sundance Film Festival experience.” (I want one of those.)
 As for the Tucci-Eisenberg gala, they are calling that “Celebrating Sundance Institute: The Boulder Debut.”
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Other soirée honorees will include Gina Prince-Bythewood (Robert Redford Luminary Award), Beth de Araújo (Vanguard Award) and Dawn Porter (Vanguard Award).
 The annual gala helps the Sundance Institute to support independent artists year-round through labs, grants and public programs that nurture artists from around the world.
 “We look forward to welcoming our community to celebrate our extraordinary honorees and champion the values that continue to guide us,” Ebs Burnough, Sundance Institute Board Chair, said in a statement.
 From left: Christopher Boeckx, Eric Mather and Seth Caikowski perform in when did the avenue theater stage the Avenue Theater’s ‘The Bible: The Complete Word of God … Abridged’ in 2007. Boeckx was just appointed to the bench in Colorado’s 18th Judicial District by Gov. Jared Polis. (The Avenue Theater) 
 How to act like a judge 
 When actor and attorney Cajardo Lindsey was appointed to the bench in Colorado’s 18th Judicial District by Gov. Jared Polis in June 2021, Colorado Politics judicial reporter Michael Karlik said Lindsey “might be the closest thing Colorado now has to a celebrity judge,” given his impressive stage and screen résumé.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 He wasn’t wrong. Lindsey has 18 screen credits and enough awards for his local stage work to fill an amphitheater. Even all that judging didn’t slow him down on stage. He somehow found time to star in the massive undertaking of Eugene O’Neill’s “A Moon for the Misbegotten.”
 Lindsey left the bench in 2024 for a place at Dan Caplis Law, which is something akin to being cast in the law iteration of the Marvel universe. And yet, he recently managed to co-star in Curious Theatre’s “Topdog/Underdog,” and he just returned from shooting a film in Tennessee.
 But wait. This is not about Lindsey. It’s about Polis’ latest announcement of the newest judge in Colorado’s very same 18th District, effective Dec. 1:
 It’s Christopher Boeckx.
 Make that: Actor and attorney Christopher Boeckx.
 As the potty-mouthed kids say: I (bleep) you not. Boeckx is replacing Lindsey’s retiring successor, Bonnie McLean. Here’s what Polis’ office is saying:
 “Boeckx is a Magistrate in the 18th Judicial District, a position he has held since 2024. His docket primarily consists of domestic-relations matters. Previously, Mr. Boeckx was a Senior Litigator at Springer and Steinberg, PC (2023-2024); Assistant Attorney General at the Colorado Attorney General’s Office …” and a whole lot more shiny stuff. Like that he earned his B.A. from Metropolitan State University of Denver in 2007 and his law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2013.
 Here’s what I am saying: Chris also played Archibald Craven in “The Secret Garden” at the Historic Elitch Theatre in 2024 And Charlie Cowell in “The Music Man” for Performance Now in Lakewood. Back in the day, he joined me in co-founding the Denver Actors Fund, which helps Colorado theater artists pay down their medical bills. After he did a tour of the Peace Corps. He’s as good as people get.
 I may be biased, but I happen to think actors make for pretty good judges.
 Jake Schroeder and Opie Gone Bad reunite at the Gothic Theatre in May 2024. (John Moore, Denver Gazette) 
 Opie Gone Back 
 I have announced approximately 3,295 final or one-off reunion shows by various bands over my career, and approximately 3,295 of them did not turn out to be final or one-offs. But that sure beats the alternative, because it means the music plays on. So I’m happy to report that the next Opie Gone Bad reunion show will take place at 8 p.m. Jan. 22 at the Gothic Theatre in Englewood. Tickets: $40 at axs.com .
 Student guitarist is mourned 
 Several communities are mourning the death of 2026 Denver School of the Arts graduate Hugh Avery. Family and friends will be celebrating his life from 1-4 p.m. on Nov. 28 in the Red Rocks Amphitheatre Visitor Center.
 Avery studied guitar at School of Rock Denver , which released a statement saying it is devastated by Avery’s death.
 “Hugh was a part of our musical community for over 10 years and leaves behind a legacy of great friendships, outstanding musicianship and deep camaraderie with our students, staff and families.”
 Bob Leggett in Vintage Theatre’s 2010 production of ‘A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum.’ (Ellen Nelson) 
 Death of an actor: Bob Leggett 
 The local theater community is mourning the death of Bob Leggett, who was active at a wide variety of area companies from 1991 to 2020. One highlight was the regional premiere of Jane Martin’s powerful abortion drama “Keely and Du” at what is now the Su Teatro Performing Arts Center (1995). Leggett was a regular at Vintage and Spotlight theaters, with credits including “You Can’t Take It with You” (2010), “Moonlight and Magnolias” (2011), “And Then There Was Nun” (2013) and “A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum” (2020). He was particularly taken with the farcical canon of Ray Cooney. He also performed with the Main Street Players, the Aurora Fox, the Evergreen Players and more.
 Leggett was diagnosed with cancer several years ago, “but he attacked this disease on his own terms, and he was determined that he would remain positive throughout this whole thing,” said Pamela Clifton, who both directed Leggett and co-starred with him.
 Two years ago, when friends thought the end was near, they held a living memorial service for Leggett at the Town Hall Arts Center. “He got to witness his own memorial – and he lived for two more years after that,” Clifton said. “Isn’t that just great?”
 John Moore is the Denver Gazette’s Senior Arts Journalist. Email him at [email protected] .
